newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-TSHWETE CALLS ON MANDELA TO TOUGHEN PROBE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-TSHWETE CALLS ON MANDELA TO TOUGHEN PROBE.

text.p: The South African government and rugby chiefs appeared locked on collision course as Sports Minister Steve Tshwete said on Monday he would appeal to President Nelson Mandela to give legal powers to a probe into the running of the game.
Tshwete said he hoped to gain permission from Mandela on Tuesday to turn the five-month old probe into the state of the game into a full judicial inquiry.
The minister has clearly lost patience with the rugby authorities, particularly its president Louis Luyt.
"I told Luyt in no unclear terms that I want him to co-operate with the task force," Tshwete told reporters.
"His instruction to the provinces is very loud. It indicates that Louis Luyt is not prepared to co-operate and is opening that avenue for me to go to the President (Mandela)."

Tshwete said he wanted the upgrading in response to the game's bosses ordering officials not to co-operate with the wide-ranging investigation which was charged with looking into every aspect, from allegations of financial misdealings to racism.
His outburst came in response to an edict issued last week by the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) telling its provincial administrators not to co-operate with the government's task force.
SARFU chief executive Rian Oberholzer gave the order, claiming the probe team was going beyond its terms of reference.

But it is just one of a number of fundamental crises facing the game. On field performances have slumped alarmingly while off the field the most powerful provincial unions are in uproar over a planned restructuring.

On the field the game is also in trouble with last Saturday's Tri-Nations defeat by Australia in Brisbane the Springboks' fourth loss in six matches this season, including their unexpected humbling by the British Lions.
There are demands for inexperienced coach Carel du Plessis to be sacked even though the 37-year-old has been in charge only since February.

Arguably even more alarming than the senior side's travails was the inept showing of the under-21 Springboks in their southern hemisphere championship where they were soundly beaten by New Zealand, Australia and, most embarrassingly, Argentina.
Off the field the game is also in danger of tearing itself apart just two years after the World Cup triumph appeared to have shaken off the game's image of apartheid at play.
A plan for South Africa to be represented by regional teams in the Super 12 has led to a revolt by four of the game's most powerful provinces.

SARFU won a majority for the scheme but Free State, Northern Transvaal, Western Province and Natal are up in arms and briefly threatened a breakaway. They claim regionalisation would dilute their identities and drive their sponsors away from the game.
Of the major unions only the Gauteng Lions, the private fiefdom of Luyt, supported the new plan.
Luyt is seen by critics within rugby as the root of all its evils. Until he is removed the game cannot go forward, they claim. However his position appears impregnable.

Son-in-law Oberholzer runs the administration and the game's executive committee appear no more than a rubber stamp. In a very rare interview in April he tellingly admitted: "I don't take a decision unless I've had it ratified."

Luyt is renowned for playing hard ball but in Tshwete he may have met his match. A Tshwete-inspired judicial inquiry into South African soccer last year led to the resignation in disgrace of its chief executive, Stix Morewa.
